title: Prehospital Equipment

source.boundary: Start at actual Prehospital Equipment title block on page 3, after Chapter 1 references. End at Chapter 2 references above actual Air Medical Transport title block on page 9. Running headers are not boundaries.
source.verification: Selected term occurrence only; not verification of current clinical guidance.

scope: Sixteen selected terms, not exhaustive chapter vocabulary. Offline candidate bank, not clinical narration or an image prompt. Repeated library/workshop terms are identified, not counted as new discoveries.

entries.cue: Two radio users, one listening and one speaking.
entries.reason: A still image shows a conversation but not both directions; could mean dispatch or online medical control. No useful distinguishing mnemonic yet.

entries.cue: A person in a familiar hazmat-style protective suit; a shield-shaped suit is an optional exaggeration.
entries.reason: Familiar protective clothing is an adequate PPE category cue. Hazmat recognition is useful, not a reason to reject the broader category. Not a specification of required equipment or protection level.

entries.cue: Large recognizable bag connected through a conspicuous valve to a face mask.
entries.reason: Three concrete name components, not a sound pun. Valve recognizability is uncertain. No patient, assembly instructions, ventilation technique or clinical benefit claim.

entries.cue: Vacuum nozzle with loose crumbs visibly gathered at its opening.
entries.reason: Familiar inward-draw association; could retrieve cleaning or vacuum rather than suction. A still image must make the nozzle-to-crumb relationship legible without relying on motion. No airway procedure or setting.

entries.cue: Tube visibly inside a transparent freestanding windpipe model.
entries.reason: Inside plus windpipe plus tube gives a learned anatomical word-part cue. Windpipe identity must be recognizable; competes with other tubes or airways. Not a placement-depth, confirmation or insertion-technique diagram; any anatomy in an actual lesson requires source verification.

entries.cue: Bellows holding an air passage open.
entries.cue_scope: Broad positive-pressure breathing-support family; requested by user as an NIPPV/CPAP recall cue, not a mode discriminator.
entries.reason: A family-level pressure/support cue can be useful when lesson context supplies the specific mode. It need not encode continuous versus bilevel to earn candidate retention. Do not infer settings, mode equivalence, delivery-interface details or clinical indications from the bellows.

entries.cue: A freestanding spine model enclosed in a clear ice block: frozen in place.
entries.reason: Spine plus frozen/no movement is a learned metaphor. Competes with spinal cooling or cold injury; explicitly exclude those readings. Never depict a patient being frozen or imply a treatment method.

entries.cue: Oversized shirt collar around a freestanding neck/spine model.
entries.reason: Collar transfers from clothing to neck-device vocabulary. Could mean ordinary clothing or neck anatomy. No recommendation, stabilization guarantee or device-fitting instruction.

entries.cue: A tractor attached by a taut rope to a separate splint prop, with no patient.
entries.reason: Tractor/traction near-sound plus pulling; not an exact homophone. Splint may be difficult to identify out of context. No force, indication, contraindication or procedural demonstration; never pull a person with a vehicle.

entries.cue: Pelvis model held steady in a broad stable cradle.
entries.reason: Pelvis plus support/stability is a conceptual association. Could mean a display stand or pelvic support, so weaker than a distinctive pun. Not a binder-placement diagram or treatment-selection rule.

entries.cue: Cartoon dynamite stick used as a learned nitro identity token.
entries.reason: Nitro/explosive association requires teaching and is not chemically exact identification of dynamite. Competes with other nitro-named drugs and explosives. Never imply medicinal formulations explode, convey handling advice or infer therapeutic effect.

entries.cue: A bronco squeezing a branching air hose visibly narrow.
entries.reason: Bronco/broncho plus squeezing supplies a learned name-and-state bridge. Could retrieve bronchoconstriction, asthma or external obstruction. Horse identity and narrowed hose must both be visible. Metaphor does not claim a literal external cause, diagnosis or treatment.
Already in the canonical offline catalog, not a new discovery. Learned name bridge, not evidence about magnetic properties, serum levels or treatment.

entries.cue: Familiar orange baking-soda box with a small heap of white powder; no brand logo or answer label needed.
entries.reason: The recognizable packaging-plus-contents association is a reasonable learned bicarbonate identity cue for this user. Judge the complete familiar object, not anonymous powder alone. Familiarity is culturally dependent, not universal. No medicinal formulation, route, dose or therapeutic use inferred.
No clear economical bridge proposed in this bounded pass. Generic emergency imagery does not distinguish the drug. Do not force sound fragments.
Repeated target, not new. Lid-cane loses spoken material and may retrieve lid or cane rather than the drug. The broadened framework does not automatically rehabilitate a weak particular sound bridge.
